stem: In which city did the League of Nations have its headquarters?

options.content: Geneva
options.rationale: Correct: in Switzerland.

options.content: New York
options.rationale: The United Nations has its headquarters in New York.

options.content: Paris
options.rationale: The Peace Conference met in Paris, but the League sat elsewhere.

options.content: London
options.rationale: The League was not based in London.

explanation: The League of Nations was based in Geneva, Switzerland.

stem: Why was the absence of the United States a weakness of the League of Nations?

options.content: The strongest economy in the world did not back sanctions or collective action
options.rationale: Correct: the League lacked its resources and influence.

options.content: The United States had been the main enemy of the League's founders in the war
options.rationale: The US president had inspired the League.

options.content: The League could not meet unless the US president was present in Geneva
options.rationale: The League met without the USA.

options.content: The United States owned the League's headquarters in Geneva and paid its staff
options.rationale: It did not.

explanation: The US Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, so the USA never joined and its economic and military strength was not behind the League.

stem: Which country was condemned by the League as the aggressor in October 1935?

options.content: Japan, for invading Manchuria
options.rationale: Japan's invasion was in 1931.

options.content: Germany, for occupying the Rhineland
options.rationale: That was in 1936 and the League took no such action.

options.content: Italy, for invading Abyssinia
options.rationale: Correct: the League imposed limited sanctions.

options.content: Greece, for entering Bulgaria
options.rationale: That was in 1925.

explanation: Italy invaded Abyssinia on 3 October 1935 and was condemned as the aggressor.

stem: Why were the sanctions imposed on Italy in 1935-36 ineffective?

options.content: They were so severe that Italy had to end the war within one week of the vote
options.rationale: Italy continued and won.

options.content: They were imposed by the United States, which controlled the whole League
options.rationale: The USA was not a member.

options.content: They left out oil, coal and steel, and the Suez Canal stayed open to Italy
options.rationale: Correct: Italy could continue the war.

options.content: They were never discussed or voted on by any of the members of the League
options.rationale: They were voted on.

explanation: Sanctions omitted oil, coal and steel, and Britain, which controlled the Suez Canal, did not close it, so Italy was able to continue.
hints: Think of the goods needed to fight a war.

stem: What was the Hoare-Laval plan of December 1935?

options.content: A plan to send the British navy to defend Abyssinia against Italy in 1935
options.rationale: No such plan existed.

options.content: A League plan to admit Germany as a permanent member of the Council in 1935 or 1936
options.rationale: Germany had joined in 1926.

options.content: A plan to give Manchuria back to China with the help of Japan and the USSR
options.rationale: This is not connected.

options.content: A British and French plan to give Italy much of Abyssinia, which then leaked
options.rationale: Correct: it showed the powers' reluctance to oppose Mussolini.

explanation: The plan, drawn up by the British and French foreign ministers, would have given Italy much of Abyssinia; when it leaked it was widely condemned.

stem: Why did the unanimity rule weaken the League of Nations?

options.content: It allowed a simple majority to force any state to send troops to the League
options.rationale: It required unanimity, not a majority.

options.content: One member could block a decision, so action was slow and avoidable
options.rationale: Correct: decisions needed the agreement of all.

options.content: It gave the Secretary-General the power to override the Council and Assembly
options.rationale: He had no such power.

options.content: It forced every member to pay exactly the same sum into the League's funds
options.rationale: That is a different matter.

explanation: Because decisions in the Council and Assembly needed agreement by all members present, any member could block action.
hints: Think about what happens if one member says no.

stem: Which statement about the League's record in the 1920s is best supported?

options.content: It prevented every dispute from becoming a war and was never defied by any state
options.rationale: It was defied at Vilna and Corfu.

options.content: It achieved nothing at all and had no staff or agencies of any kind in Geneva
options.rationale: It had agencies and some successes.

options.content: It was ended in 1920 when the United States withdrew from it for good
options.rationale: It lasted until 1946.

options.content: It settled small disputes and did humanitarian work, but could not make great powers obey
options.rationale: Correct: it shows both success and limit.

explanation: The League resolved disputes such as Aaland and Greece-Bulgaria and did humanitarian work, but Poland at Vilna and Italy at Corfu defied it.
hints: Look for a statement that weighs success and failure.

stem: Which point best supports the view that the self-interest of Britain and France was a major cause of the League's failure?

options.content: The United States refused to join the League after the vote in the Senate in 1919
options.rationale: This is about the USA, not Britain and France.

options.content: They chose weak sanctions over Abyssinia, hoping to keep Mussolini as an ally
options.rationale: Correct: they placed their own interests above collective security.

options.content: Japan left the League in 1933 after the report on its actions in Manchuria
options.rationale: This shows an aggressor leaving.

options.content: The League had no army of its own and relied on the members for force
options.rationale: This shows a structural weakness.

explanation: Britain and France preferred weak sanctions and the Hoare-Laval plan because they hoped to keep Italy as an ally against Germany.
hints: Choose the point that concerns the decisions of Britain and France.

stem: The League of Nations was dissolved in 1946, after the creation of the United Nations.
explanation: The League was formally dissolved in April 1946, and the UN took over many of its functions.

explanation: The US Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, and the USA never joined.

points.description: To prevent war through collective security
To encourage disarmament
To settle disputes by negotiation and arbitration
To improve living and working conditions around the world

It showed that the League would not protect an African state against a European aggressor, which weakened the League and encouraged anti-colonial feeling

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a speech by a fictional delegate of a small state at the League Assembly, 1936 (invented for this question)

> A small state that trusts the Covenant is today told that the Covenant cannot protect it. If we allow an aggressor to take a member's land and then reward him by proposing terms, we teach every ambitious government that force pays. The League will then be only a debating society.

**Source B** — a private note by a fictional British official, 1935 (invented for this question)

> We cannot risk a naval war in the Mediterranean for the sake of Abyssinia. The League is useful, but it is not worth losing Italy as a friend in Europe, where the real danger lies in Germany. Sanctions must be limited to what we can safely enforce.

That the League will become only a debating society / force will be rewarded

parts.stem: How far do the sources help to explain why the League failed over Abyssinia?

points.description: A shows the small states' view that failure to act encourages aggressors, and the damage to the League's credibility
B shows the self-interest of a leading member, which preferred a friendly Italy and avoided war
Provenance: A is a public speech meant to persuade; B is a private note and so likely to be frank about motives

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The sources help to explain the failure from two sides. Source A, a public speech by a small state's delegate, shows how failure to act would encourage aggressors and reduce the League to a debating society. Source B, a private note by a British official, shows that a leading member put its own interests first, avoiding a naval war and hoping to keep Italy as a friend against Germany. Because B is private it is likely to be frank about motives, while A is meant to persuade. My own knowledge confirms that the sanctions excluded oil, the Suez Canal stayed open, and the Hoare-Laval plan was leaked.

explanation: Both sources are invented: a delegate's speech and an official's private note.
hints: For (c), contrast a public speech with a private note.

stem: To what extent was the Abyssinian crisis the main reason for the failure of the League of Nations?

points.description: The crisis: Italy invaded in October 1935, weak sanctions, Hoare-Laval plan, Addis Ababa fell in May 1936, loss of confidence
Earlier failures: Vilna, Corfu, Manchuria 1931-33 and the leaving of Japan and Germany
Structural weaknesses: no USA, no army, unanimity, the link with Versailles
Other factors: the Depression, dictators, self-interest of Britain and France
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The Abyssinian crisis was a major reason for the League's failure, but it was the result of deeper weaknesses. Italy invaded Abyssinia in October 1935, and the weak sanctions, which excluded oil, and the Hoare-Laval plan showed that Britain and France would not stop a great power, so small states lost faith and Italy completed the conquest in 1936. But the League had been defied earlier, at Vilna and Corfu and by Japan in Manchuria, and Japan and Germany had already left it. Its structure was weak, since the USA never joined, it had no army and decisions needed unanimity. The Depression and the rise of dictators made states pursue their own interests. I conclude that Abyssinia was the clearest demonstration of the League's failure and destroyed its credibility, but the main causes were the structural weaknesses and the self-interest of its leading members, which had been clear since 1931.

explanation: Credit the crisis, earlier failures, structural weaknesses and a supported judgement.
hints: Compare a turning point with long-term weaknesses.

stem: Assess the successes of the League of Nations in the 1920s.

points.description: Disputes: Aaland Islands (1921), Upper Silesia, Greece and Bulgaria (1925)
Humanitarian work: prisoners of war, refugees and the Nansen passport, health, drugs, slavery, the ILO
Limits: Vilna and Corfu, where great powers defied the League; the work depended on goodwill
Judgement on how successful it was

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; balance is attempted and a judgement is reached, but it is only partly supported or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The League had real successes in the 1920s, especially with smaller states and in humanitarian work. It settled the Aaland Islands dispute in 1921 and ordered Greek troops out of Bulgaria in 1925. It returned prisoners of war, helped refugees through the Nansen passport and worked against disease, drugs and slavery, and the International Labour Organization set standards for work. But it could not make great powers obey, as shown at Vilna and Corfu, and its successes depended on the goodwill of the parties. I conclude that the League was fairly successful in the 1920s with minor disputes and social work, but had not yet been tested by a determined great power.

explanation: Credit explained successes, limits and a judgement.
hints: Separate political successes from humanitarian ones.
